title-group.article-title: Building Australia’s National Reserve System for 30 × 30: A Critique of New Biodiversity Datasets and Prioritization Frameworks, and Suggested Improvements to Achieve Effective Outcomes

abstract.p: In 2022, Australia became a signatory to the Convention on Biological Diversity’s Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which included commitments to contribute to restoration of 30% of all degraded ecosystems (Target 2) and the achievement of at least 30% protection and conservation of land and seas by 2030 (Target 3). As part of its response towards delivering on Target 3, the Australian Government released its ‘National Roadmap for Protecting and Conserving 30% of Australia’s Land by 2030’ in 2024, which has underpinned subsequent policy and program development. As part of these initiatives, the Australian Government published a technical report in early 2026 prepared by Environment Information Australia to identify priority locations for the protection and conservation of biodiversity, including opportunities to enhance the representativeness of Australia’s protected areas. Here, we review the policy context for these prioritizations and assess how well the spatial prioritization framework, objectives, data, and outputs respond to these policy needs. We outline several fundamental concerns with the approach, including that the prioritization framework was not designed around measurable planning objectives; instead, “components” to be scored are identified, but no targets or outcomes are set against which the maps could be tested; and that it deviates from the science-based approach which has been used to identify priorities for addition to the National Reserve System since the mid-1990s. We also raise concerns about the data used within the spatial prioritization, and the implications for achieving 30 × 30 outcomes in the most effective way possible if the prioritization approach from this technical assessment continues to be applied in its current form. Given that the assessment is informing decisions about where to invest in ecosystem protection, enhancement and restoration, we conclude with some recommendations to help guide a revised version of the technical assessment and associated mapping outputs as soon as possible.

funding-group.funding-statement: This research received no external funding.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Since the mid-1990s, in response to its commitments under the 1992 Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), Australia has had a nationally agreed, science-based approach to expanding its protected area estate. Principles of Comprehensiveness, Adequacy and Representativeness (CAR) were embedded into national policies and programs such as the Regional Forest Agreement processes [1] and the National Reserve System (NRS) [2,3,4,5] (Table 1). They remain central to Australia’s Strategy for the National Reserve System 2009–2030 (the ‘NRS Strategy’) and Australia’s Strategy for Nature 2024–2030 [6]. The CAR criteria have also underpinned protected area planning and biodiversity conservation in multiple jurisdictions in Australia, e.g., [7,8,9,10,11,12,13]. The CBD’s Aichi Target 11 (2010–2020) and the more recent Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework’s (GBF) Target 3 (2022–2030) not only increased the ambition of the spatial coverage of what was expected of Parties to the CBD but also outlined the features that protected and conserved area networks should protect and the ways they should be implemented.

Target 3 of the GBF (commonly termed the ‘30 × 30 target’) articulates how signatory nations are expected to expand and manage protected and conserved area systems as follows: “ensure and enable that by 2030 at least 30 percent of terrestrial and inland water areas and of coastal and marine areas, especially areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services, are effectively conserved and managed through ecologically representative, well-connected and equitably governed systems of protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures, recognizing indigenous and traditional territories where applicable, and integrated into wider landscapes, seascapes and the ocean, while ensuring that any sustainable use, where appropriate in such areas, is fully consistent with conservation outcomes, recognizing and respecting the rights of indigenous peoples and local communities, including over their traditional territories” [14].

As part of Australia’s response to this international commitment and policy guidance, in 2024 the Australian Government published its National Roadmap for Protecting and Conserving 30% of Australia’s Land by 2030 (the ‘Roadmap’), which sets out priorities and methods for achieving 30 × 30 [15]. The Roadmap is an overarching framework that complements Australia’s Strategy for the National Reserve System 2009–2030 [5], Australia’s Strategy for Nature 2024–2030 [6], the National Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (OECM) Framework [16], and relevant policies in each state and territory.

A technical report ‘Identifying biodiversity value and potential to enhance the representativeness of Australia’s protected areas using Multi-criteria Decision Analysis, version 1.0’ and associated online maps (https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/6386bf14a5d7448e96b682483842a25d/, accessed on 3 March 2026) were prepared by Environment Information Australia (EIA) for the Australian Government’s Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) [17] and released in January 2026. The technical report details the methods used by EIA to develop three map layers relevant to the two criteria developed to identify priority areas for 30 × 30 in the Roadmap (Table 2). These layers comprised: (1) Criterion 1—areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services; (2) Criterion 2—areas that enhance ecological comprehensiveness and representativeness; and (3) Criteria 1 and 2 combined.

As described by DCCEEW [18], the maps represent “…new tools to help guide our work to protect and conserve 30% of Australia’s land by 2030… (They) highlight areas known to have important biodiversity and ecosystem values that are not well represented in our existing protected areas… The maps help identify places where protection or conservation can make the greatest difference for long-term biodiversity outcomes… and (They) are one of several tools that will inform national environmental priorities, including the $250 million Australian Bushland Program”. The Australian Government’s Seventh National Report to the Convention on Biological Diversity [19] stated: “In addition to reaching 30%, it is important to protect and conserve the ‘right’ areas…. The new spatial products will help guide decision making and are intended to be used alongside regional and local scale information”. Given this context, it is critical that the data and methods used are robust, and that decisions are made cognisant of the limitations of the current maps and data underpinning the maps.

This review paper provides a critique of the data inputs, methods, and output maps from the technical report against the existing, nationally agreed framework for identifying priority areas for inclusion in the National Reserve System [5]. The assessment is also based on our collective, long history of using ecological datasets and planning tools to inform the location of new protected areas (and protected area networks) [7,8,20,21,22,23,24,25], and in science-based protected area policy and guidance at state, national and international levels [3,4,26,27,28]. We describe why we consider that this technical assessment and associated map outputs are not fit for purpose against the stated policy and conservation-planning objectives in their current form, and risk channeling investment towards places of lower conservation priority. Our central argument is that the prioritization was not designed around the planning objectives it is intended to deliver (e.g., “help identify places where protection or conservation can make the greatest difference for long-term biodiversity outcomes” [18]) and the concerns we raise about individual components and datasets follow from that. Noting that the maps and report represent the first iteration of this prioritization process, the purpose of this review paper is to assist with short- and medium-term improvements to the integrity of the mapping and to inform government policies and programs that might be influenced by these maps. Our evaluation was based on details contained in the EIA [17] document and output maps; we did not perform separate spatial analyses. As our conclusions are based on the published EIA documentation and maps, we acknowledge that not all underlying datasets and modeling assumptions may necessarily have been made available in those products, and that our review does not constitute an independent spatial validation of the national mapping outputs.

sec.title: 2. Review of Methodological Approach
sec.p: Fundamental to the implementation of Target 3 of the GBF are the guiding principles that new protected and conserved areas should be: ecologically representative, well connected, integrated into the wider landscape, and effectively and equitably managed, with emphasis on areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services [14]. Many of these same conservation planning principles have underpinned policy for the identification of priority ecosystems and areas for addition to the National Reserve System for the past 30 years [1,3,4,5]. Furthermore, these principles have been used as part of many spatial conservation planning processes to help identify parcels of land that most efficiently complement the existing protected area network in terms of ecosystem and species representation [12,29].

By comparison, the methods applied by EIA [17] do not incorporate all components of the CAR criteria, nor the specific targets set in the NRS Strategy [5] for progressing a CAR reserve system by 2030 (Table 1). Although the EIA [17] approach is broader, covering aspects of Target 3 of the GBF, it did not state why nationally agreed approaches to measuring CAR were not followed despite national datasets being available to enable consistent approaches. More detailed analyses of these differences are provided in Section 3 and Section 4 below.

sec.title: Spatial Prioritization Framework
sec.p: The spatial prioritization methods used for each Roadmap criterion (Table 2) were based on a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) approach. This approach, used by EIA [17], assigned a score for each of the measured components and then added these individual component scores together to provide an overall ‘value’ score for each criterion. The combined criteria map then added up the overall scores from Criterion 1 and Criterion 2 for every 250 m × 250 m pixel and rescaled that total score from 0 to 1.

The assessment method did not use systematic conservation planning methods such as complementarity, where new priority areas are meant to be identified to complement what is already protected [12], and landscape-planning approaches to maximize connectivity between existing protected areas [30,31]. Instead, the EIA [17] approach overlaid many complex datasets into single cumulative scores for biodiversity value at a pixel scale of 250 m × 250 m across the Australian continent that does not consider complementarity or connectivity. In so doing, it deviates substantially from the long-standing approach set out in Australia’s Strategy for the National Reserve System 2009–2030 [5] and strategies prior to that [3,4].

A technical issue with the EIA [17] MCDA method is that each component was weighted equally, rather than weighted differentially. The ecological or policy rationale for equal weighting was not documented. This approach differs from most applications of MCDA for conservation planning, where one of the critical steps in the planning process is bringing stakeholders together to assign different weights to relevant biodiversity features to achieve agreed conservation objectives as effectively as possible (e.g., [32]).

As detailed below, under Criterion 1, the MCDA approach applied by the EIA [17] has some further, inherent and significant problems because of:(1)
Differences in the reliability of the data inputs;(2)
The selection of some of the data input layers not representing good surrogates for a value (e.g., datasets contributing to the ecosystem services component);(3)
The double-use of some values in different datasets creating compounding or ‘double-counting’ effects (e.g., threatened species potentially being scored under ‘species diversity’, ‘endemism’, ‘threatened species’ and ‘migratory species’);(4)
The assignment of equal weight to components which are assessing very different aspects of biodiversity importance (e.g., landscape connectivity versus endemism hotspots).
The following sections detail our concerns with some of the data inputs and methods relating to each criterion and associated map outputs.

sec.title: 3. Criterion 1: Areas of Particular Importance for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Functions and Services
sec.p: Criterion 1 comprises six components. These components are taken from the Roadmap (Table 2), with the caveat that the EIA [17] assessment method combines two separate components included in the Roadmap [15] (i.e., ecological integrity and ecological connectivity). In the EIA’s approach, each of these components was weighted equally, and the scores for each component were then combined into a single Criterion 1 score. Combined scores were then assigned to six categories of overall biodiversity value. The map of Criterion 1 values is shown in Figure 1.

sec.title: 3.1. Limitations of the Criterion 1 Assessment Framework
sec.p: The six components identify what is valued under Criterion 1, but no measurable objective or target is set for any of them, so there is no benchmark against which the choice of components, datasets and weightings can be judged. Several limitations of the Criterion 1 framework relate to the overall assessment methodology in addition to the individual components. Although the six components broadly align with priorities identified in the Roadmap [15], they do not fully represent all biodiversity priorities identified in the NRS Strategy [5], including critical habitat for threatened species and ecological communities at the bioregional level and areas important for climate resilience. Consequently, some nationally significant biodiversity values are likely to be underrepresented in the maps.

The assessment also relies heavily on modeled datasets, resulting in substantial spatial variation in data quality and confidence. This may be particularly important in data-poor regions such as Australia’s outback region, where more than half of the continent has been assigned to the lowest biodiversity value category despite the recognized ecological importance of much of this landscape [33].

All of the individual components aggregate multiple biodiversity attributes into composite measures. While this simplifies implementation, it reduces transparency, limits interpretation of the drivers of site importance, and increases the potential for double counting where biodiversity values overlap. The aggregation of multiple input layers related to the different components further reduces the accuracy of the overall summary layer of biodiversity values, as some of the individual layers identify very different parts of Australia as being important for biodiversity values.

In some cases, distinct ecological concepts, such as habitat condition and ecological connectivity, have been combined within a single assessment component, despite these being recognized as separate aspects of protected and conserved area planning under GBF Target 3 [14] and the National Roadmap [15].

The ‘ecosystem functions and services’ component conflates ecosystem services with ecosystem functions—which are distinct concepts and qualities [34]—and draws on datasets (volumetric water capacity, soil nitrogen, soil phosphorus, soil carbon) of unclear purpose and uneven national coverage. As such, this component is conceptually inconsistent in what it contributes to a biodiversity prioritization process. The definitions of both protected areas and Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (OECMs) focus on the conservation of biodiversity, and ecosystem functions and services are “associated” with biodiversity qualities under these definitions [34]. Based on this explanation, we suggest that further work is needed to clearly define what is meant by these terms before they are assessed for their relevance to the identification of priority biodiversity areas in Australia. A more useful approach would be to identify priority areas for the respective ecosystem services, once these have been clearly defined.

Finally, the classification approach further reduces discrimination among low-scoring areas by grouping all scores below 50 into a single category. Retaining finer score intervals (e.g., 10-point quantiles) across the full range of scores would improve discrimination among lower-scoring areas.

sec.title: 3.2. Improvements Suggested
sec.p:
If continuing with a MCDA approach, short-term priorities for improvement include:
Disaggregating the input components so that they are scored and mapped individually, not as a single, combined measure of overall biodiversity value.
Disaggregating the input layers contributing to some of the component scores (e.g., for threatened ecological communities and threatened species, and for habitat condition and connectivity) so that the information is clearer and more robust.
Mapping or documenting data quality and confidence for each layer.
Removing component 5 (ecosystem functions and services) from the set of data inputs. Use of such layers needs to be bolstered with more biodiversity-relevant services (e.g., carbon in natural ecosystems) and treated as a separate map to biodiversity values. Greater clarity on how ecosystem functions are defined and mapped is required.

Ideally, the government should define measurable objectives and targets for each criterion up front, and then should use systematic conservation planning methods and associated decision-support tools, including spatial prioritization [12,35], to achieve the more robust identification of areas important for biodiversity conservation in Australia. Longer-term improvements should also focus on improving the selection and standards of national biodiversity datasets.

sec.title: 4. Criterion 2: Areas That Enhance Ecological Comprehensiveness and Representativeness
sec.p: In the EIA [17] approach, Criterion 2 focuses on representativeness of ecosystems within protected areas at a bioregional and subregional scale (bioregions and subregions as defined in the Interim Biogeographic Regionalization for Australia (IBRA) [2]. It does this by calculating for every bioregional/subregional ecosystem (based on Major Vegetation Groups (MVGs) within the National Vegetation Information System [36]), (a) the proportion of their current extent within each bioregion/subregion which is protected and (b) the proportion remaining of their pre-1750 extent.

An inverse scoring method is then applied that assigns higher priority to ecosystems with low remaining vegetation extent or low protection, ensuring those ecosystems receive higher weight. The final unified score is developed by summing, for each 250 m cell, the inverse scores obtained for the two components at a bioregional scale and at a subregional scale (i.e., 4 scores) and then scaling those summed scores. This process is done for each ecosystem present that intersects with the cell, and those results are summed and then rescaled between 0 and 1000. The final outputs map is shown in Figure 2.

sec.title: 4.1. Limitations of the Criterion 2 Assessment Framework

list-item.p: Conceptually, this approach is reasonably well aligned with CAR criteria for comprehensiveness and representativeness. We note, however, that the output map combines measures of ecosystem depletion and ecosystem representation in the protected area network into a single score. As depletion and representation are quite different ecological attributes of an ecosystem, they should be kept separate. The method also combines assessments of ecosystem representation at an IBRA bioregional scale and at an IBRA subregional scale into a single score, whereas the NRS Strategy [5] approach is to keep these measures separate (Table 1), as indicators of comprehensiveness and representativeness, respectively. The Roadmap [15] also makes this distinction by separating bioregion and subregion under its Representativeness criterion (Table 2).

The method used to assess ecosystem representation in the protected area network is not consistent with previous iterations used to assess ecosystem representation in Australia under past and current policy [1,5]. Protection is measured as the proportion of each ecosystem example already within protected areas, but no measure is included of the extent of each bioregion within protected areas, which is one of the targets for comprehensiveness in the NRS Strategy [5] (Table 1), and no target is set against which either measure could be assessed. The output map accordingly seems to show little differentiation between the significance scores assigned to ecosystems in some bioregions that have very different levels of remnant vegetation and protection. For example, the Goldfields subregion of the Victorian Midlands bioregion in central Victoria, where there is >50% remnant native vegetation and 9.9% protection, appears to have similar overall priority scores under Criterion 2 to the Victorian Riverina subregion (Figure 3), despite the Victorian Riverina subregion containing only 19.2% remnant native vegetation and 3.3% of land under formal protection [37,38]. The Highlands—Northern Fall subregion likewise scores highly under this criterion, despite much higher levels of both native vegetation (68.8%; [37]) and protected area coverage (23%; [38]), compared to the Monaro subregion (8.7% protected) (Figure 3). These examples show how this current prioritization approach risks directing conservation effort towards areas that are already well vegetated and well protected, rather than towards the most depleted and least protected ecosystems.

sec.title: 4.2. Suggested Improvements
sec.p: In the longer term, we also recommend that the government needs to address the Adequacy component of the CAR criteria, for example by setting explicit representation targets (e.g., % of current or pre-1750 extent protected, rather than an ambiguous ‘sample’) for every bioregional/subregional ecosystem. As stated already under Criterion 1, we also recommend the application of existing systematic conservation planning approaches and decision-support tools to optimize identification of priority areas for addition to the protected/conserved estate, as has happened in many other parts of the globe [35].

sec.title: 5. Combined Criteria: Biodiversity Values and Representativeness
sec.p: Combined values were developed for every cell by summing their Criterion 1 and Criterion 2 scores and then rescaling combined results from 0 to 1000 (Figure 4).

There are two major concerns with this approach and the map. Firstly, Criterion 1 often scores more highly for ecosystems that are part of extensive areas of native vegetation, while Criterion 2 scores more highly for ecosystems that have been highly cleared and/or poorly reserved. So, a site that is part of a well-protected, well-vegetated landscape will score highly under Criterion 1 and poorly under Criterion 2. When the results are combined, a medium score is generated, which then becomes the default for remnant ecosystem patches across many different bioregions in Australia, severely diminishing its usefulness to inform protection priorities. Secondly, the map tries to combine two different and distinct components (and objectives) of a protected/conserved area system—an ecologically representative reserve system and a reserve system which protects important places for biodiversity. These are different concepts, as articulated in GBF Target 3, and in the NRS Strategy and Roadmap. None of these documents, nor science, suggests they be combined in this way. Accordingly, the methods and layers should be discrete.
We recommend that the combined map layer not be used for decision-making or investment decisions as it currently stands.

sec.title: 6. Discussion
sec.p: The development of new biodiversity layers to inform the expansion of Australia’s protected and conserved area estate to meet the different ecological elements of the 30 × 30 target is needed and welcomed. It is also recognized that such layers will evolve and be updated over time as better data and knowledge come to hand, as has been the case for layers influential in the expansion of Australia’s National Reserve System over time (e.g., bioregions (IBRA) and vegetation types (NVIS)) (e.g., [11,13,28,39,40]). However, based on our review of the methods, data inputs and map-layer outputs developed by EIA [17] to help identify 30 × 30 priorities in Australia, we recommend caution in using the current assessment and maps to guide investments in new protected areas and other relevant targets under Australia’s Strategy for Nature [6], including restoration and species conservation. As outlined above, we do not consider that the individual maps relating to Criteria 1 and 2 are adequately supported by the current data and methodology. We furthermore do not consider it at all appropriate to combine Criteria 1 and 2 data layers into a single combined map of ‘biodiversity values’ across Australia. We suggest that a ‘version 2’ is urgently needed, which improves both the data inputs and the methods applied. In their current form, we believe the maps are not fit for purpose to inform 30 × 30 target delivery in a way which systematically helps build the NRS and its complementary network of conserved areas. As it is, use of the maps for decision-making and investment runs the risk of prioritizing investment in low-priority places, and a lack of investment in areas which are priorities for protection. Although DCCEEW and EIA have stated the maps were a ‘first iteration’ and would be updated over time, no such timeline has been proposed.

The necessary refinement of priority maps as recommended should not delay the roll-out of associated investment programs, such as the $250 million Australian Bushland Program. Indeed, with only four years remaining to meet the 30 × 30 target and with 22.57% of land protected based on published 2024 data ([38], although approximately 25% in mid-2026 based on government announcements [41]), there is still significant progress needed. Notwithstanding these policy and program imperatives, we recommend that, at a minimum, the various components of Criteria 1 and 2 be disaggregated into separate maps and separate priorities so that it is clear to decision-makers and investors as to what is important and where, and that the combined biodiversity values and representativeness map be removed from the website.

In the medium term, we recommend that, for those components for which there is no agreed national approach for assessing spatial priorities for protection, restoration or species’ conservation (e.g., connectivity mapping, ecosystem function mapping, restoration priorities), governments and stakeholders work together to develop appropriate methods and datasets. In addition, we recommend that further work be done with experts and relevant stakeholders to identify the biodiversity values and datasets that are most useful for contributing to mapping under both criteria, and that systematic conservation planning tools be considered to assist with spatial prioritization of where best to protect and conserve biodiversity. It will also be critical to state, for each criterion, the planning objective it is intended to achieve and the measure by which achievement would be judged. The choice of components, datasets and method should then follow from that objective.

Finally, we note that some of the issues we have identified with these layers stem from a lack of agreed definitions and standards in policy and science-based spatial datasets to identify areas of particular importance for biodiversity, ecosystem functions, ecosystem services and connectivity. There is a wealth of science and practical experience in Australia in developing and using ecological datasets for prioritizing and establishing protected and conserved area networks which are as efficient and as effective as possible, e.g., [12,35,42]. We encourage the Australian Government to draw on this extensive knowledge and experience base to help improve 30 × 30 outcomes and achieve the greatest biodiversity gains possible.

caption.p: Criteria to identify priority areas for 30 × 30 as listed in the National Roadmap for protecting and conserving 30% of Australia’s land by 2030 [15].

tr.td: (1) Areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services

Priority should be given to areas that:·
are high in species diversity·
contain species that are highly endemic to an area·
provide habitat for nationally listed threatened species and ecological communities, and migratory species·
contain, or provide habitat for, species and/or ecological communities under severe and imminent threat, that are irreplaceable, and/or at risk of extinction·
are important for the continued provision of ecosystem functions and services·
have ecological integrity and intactness·
contribute to ecological connectivity.
(2) Areas that enhance ecological comprehensiveness and representativeness
Alignment with the CAR scientific framework. Priority should be given to including adequate samples of ecosystems within and across each IBRA bioregion and subregion.
